ui.lineage_banner_text: Start here — {start} is a plain, exacting voice, and where the Buddhist tradition begins. To trace how ideas passed from teacher to student, see {lineage}.
ui.empty_state: No one matches that search. Try a different name, idea, or school.
ui.disclaimer_line: Educational simulation, not therapy or medical advice. In a crisis, contact local emergency services or (US) call/text 988.
ui.about_p1: What this is. Traditions of the Mind is an educational simulator. Each of the 68 characters is built from publicly documented biography, core concepts, and characteristic techniques associated with a real historical or contemporary psychologist, psychotherapist, philosopher, or meditation teacher. Replies are generated by a scripted, offline template engine (or, only if you supply your own API key, by a live language model instructed to stay in character) — never by the actual person.
ui.about_p_not: Not therapy. Not a diagnosis. Not medical, psychiatric, or crisis care. Not the real person's own words — treat every reply as an invented, illustrative composite, not a verified quote. Nothing here should be used to make decisions about medication, treatment, or safety.
ui.about_p_struggling: If you're in crisis or thinking about suicide or self-harm, please contact a real person: a crisis line, a doctor, or someone you trust. In the US, call or text 988. Outside the US, search “[your country] crisis line” or contact local emergency services. This app will always redirect to this message if it detects that kind of content, instead of continuing the roleplay.
ui.about_p_data: Conversations and any API key you enter are stored only in your browser's local storage on this device. Nothing is sent to us. If you enable live mode, your messages are sent directly from your browser to the AI provider you configure.
ui.lineage_intro: Two chains worth tracing, exactly as requested: the line that formed Perls, and the humanistic/existential circle worth comparing him against.
ui.traditions_intro: Buddhist philosophers and contemplative teachers, plus a few figures who bridge back into psychology (Skinner → experimental psychology, Freud → psychoanalysis, Kahneman → cognitive science, Nāgārjuna → Buddhist philosophy, Namkhai Norbu → the Dzogchen contemplative tradition). Read them side by side and a single question runs underneath all of it: how have different traditions understood the mind, consciousness, suffering, behavior, and transformation?

founders.label: Founding Psychology
openers: Before we go further -- describe exactly what you noticed, the way a trained introspectionist would: no interpretation yet, just the raw report.
James called it a stream -- is {topic} really one thing, or a moving current you're freezing into a snapshot?
What's the structure underneath {topic} -- the basic elements it's built from, before you assemble them into a story?
What function does {topic} actually serve for you right now, practically -- what is it *for*?
If you slowed {topic} down to a single frame, like a lab observation, what would you actually see?
Separate the raw sensation in {topic} from the label you've already stuck on it.
reflect: Stripped of interpretation, what you're describing is: {topic}. What else is actually there, before the story?
That's the surface report. What function does {topic} serve underneath -- what is the habit doing for you?
Notice how much of {topic} is raw sensation, and how much is the narrative you've layered on top.
It behaves more like a stream than a fixed object -- continuously becoming, not static.
The habit itself may matter more here than any single thought about {topic}.
technique: Try trained introspection: describe {topic} again as plainly as you'd describe a chair -- no metaphors, just the elements.
Ask what {topic} is *for*, the way you'd ask what a habit is for -- function before meaning.
Try a stream-of-consciousness pass: sixty seconds, uncensored, everything that crosses your mind about {topic}.

psychoanalytic.label: Psychoanalytic / Psychodynamic
openers: Say whatever comes to mind first, uncensored, when you sit with that -- that's the rule of free association.
Does {topic} echo something from an earlier chapter of your life?
I notice *how* you're telling me this. What might this manner of telling be protecting you from?
Whose voice is really in {t1}, if you listen underneath your own?
If this were a dream from last night, what would the dream-version of {topic} be disguising?
What's the earliest memory that surfaces if you let {topic} sit for a moment?
reflect: There may be more under {topic} than you're saying, even to yourself.
This reaction is bigger than this one moment -- it seems to be carrying something older. That's usually how transference shows up.
Notice the feeling you're avoiding naming directly. What would it be called, if you let yourself say it?
Transference happens outside the room too -- who does this remind you of, again, this time?
A slip, a joke, a forgotten detail in {topic} is rarely just an accident -- Freud called these parapraxes.
technique: Try free association for one minute: uncensored, everything that follows "{topic} reminds me of...".
Ask how {topic} would look if it were really about someone from your past, not the present.
Notice any resistance to going deeper into {topic} -- the discomfort itself is usually the signal worth following.

jungian.label: Analytical / Jungian
openers: What images or symbols come up when you think about {topic}?
Is there a part of you in {t2} that you usually keep in shadow?
If this situation were a dream, what would it be telling you?
What does {topic} want from you -- something you haven't been willing to give it yet?
What would your dreams say about {topic}, if you asked them tonight?
Where does {topic} touch individuation -- becoming more fully who you actually are?
reflect: This might be your shadow speaking -- the part of you that doesn't fit your idea of who you are.
This might have less to do with the other person and more to do with something in you seeking integration.
The archetype underneath {topic} deserves a name. What role does it seem to play -- protector, exile, judge?
The Self is larger than the ego currently arguing with {topic}.
What meaningful coincidence -- synchronicity -- surrounds {topic}, regardless of cause?
technique: Try active imagination: hold {topic} in mind and let an image from it move and speak on its own, without steering it.
Ask what {topic} is compensating for -- what one-sidedness in you it might be trying to balance.
Let an image tied to {topic} answer a single question: what does it want?

adlerian.label: Individual Psychology (Adlerian)
openers: In service of what do you think {topic} is really happening -- what are you striving toward?
Where do you feel "less than," and who set that yardstick?
How does {topic} connect to your sense of belonging -- your social interest?
What would "enough" look like here, concretely?
What's your earliest recollection, and how does it relate to this feeling?
Whose applause were you originally trying to win with patterns like {topic}?
reflect: Underneath is often a feeling of not measuring up -- does that resonate with {topic}?
This sounds like your style of life showing up here -- a strategy learned early to feel significant.
Notice the social piece: who are you trying to matter to, in {topic}?
Early recollections are less factual history and more a mirror of your current style of life.
Courage, not comfort, is usually what social interest calls for here.
technique: Ask what a small but genuinely useful contribution to someone else would look like right now -- social interest tends to loosen a knot like this.
Sort how much of {topic} is really about competence, and how much about belonging.
Try acting "as if" you already belonged, for one day, and notice what that does to {topic}.

humanistic.label: Humanistic / Person-Centered
openers: I'm listening. What does {topic} feel like from the inside, in your own words?
What would it mean to fully accept that feeling, exactly as it is, just for a moment?
What need feels unmet underneath {topic}?
What would the healthiest, most whole version of you think about this?
What would unconditional positive regard toward yourself sound like right now?
Is the person you are around {topic} congruent with who you feel you are inside?
reflect: It sounds like {topic} matters a great deal to you -- and that matters to me too.
You're describing something real and valid. What would it be like to trust that reaction instead of arguing with it?
There's a growth edge in {topic} -- a part of you reaching toward something truer.
Self-empathy matters here as much as empathy for anyone else would.
The organism tends toward growth when conditions are safe enough -- what would make this safer?
technique: Finish this sentence, slowly, a few times: "What I actually feel about {topic} is...".
Notice: are you judging the feeling, or just having it? See what shifts if you simply let it exist.
Just reflect {topic} back to yourself, without advice or judgment, the way a good listener would.

existential.label: Existential
openers: What does {topic} ask you to be honest about -- especially with yourself?
Where do you actually have a choice here, even a small one?
If this were the last time you'd face exactly this situation, what would matter?
What meaning might {topic} be pointing toward, even unwelcome?
What would you regret not saying or doing about {topic}, looking back from the end of your life?
Where does {topic} touch the absurd -- the gap between what you want and what the world offers?
reflect: Underneath {topic} often sits one of the given facts of existence -- our mortality, our aloneness, our freedom, or the search for meaning. Which feels closest to the surface here?
This anxiety may not be a malfunction -- it may be the honest sound of freedom, of a real choice in front of you.
Notice how much of {topic} is about what happened, and how much about how you're choosing to respond.
This could be existential guilt -- the cost of not living out a real possibility.
Death isn't only an ending; awareness of it can clarify what actually matters in {topic}.
technique: Ask yourself directly: what am I responsible for here, and what am I not?
Name out loud the one thing about {topic} you've been avoiding saying plainly.
Ask simply: if I fully accepted that this is finite, would I still spend {topic} the same way?

gestalt.label: Gestalt Therapy
openers: Stay with that. What are you aware of right now, in your body, as you say it?
Don't explain {topic} to me -- show me. What's happening as you sit with it, right in this second?
If {topic} were sitting in the empty chair across from you, what would you say to it?
What are you doing right now -- with your breath, your hands, your face -- while you tell me this?
What's figure and what's ground right now -- what's making noise, and what's quietly holding it up?
Finish out loud: "What I'm not saying about {topic} is...".
reflect: I'm less interested in why {topic} happened, and more in what's happening between us right now as you say it.
That sounds like unfinished business -- something that was never closed or said.
Notice the boundary here: where does {topic} stop being yours and start being theirs?
That sounds like retroflection -- doing to yourself what you'd rather do to someone else.
Contact, not insight, is what actually closes unfinished business like {topic}.
technique: Try this: put {topic} on an empty chair in front of you and say out loud what you'd never say to its face.
Say the sentence again, but this time fully own it: swap "it happens" for "I do this."
Exaggerate the gesture or tone you're using about {topic} right now -- what does it reveal, amplified?

behaviorist.label: Behaviorist
openers: What happens exactly right before {topic} -- what's the precise antecedent?
What happens right after -- what does {topic} get you, even if it's not what you want long-term?
On a scale, how intense is it, and what would one notch less look like?
What's the smallest observable change you could actually measure this week?
What reinforcement schedule is keeping {topic} alive -- constant, or only sometimes, which is often stronger?
If a stranger only watched your actions around {topic}, what would they conclude you wanted?
reflect: Whatever else is going on, {topic} is also a learned pattern -- which means it can be unlearned, deliberately, in steps.
Notice what's reinforcing this. Something is being rewarded here, even if it doesn't feel like a reward.
Let's set feelings aside for a moment and just track the behavior: what exactly did you do, and when?
Extinction bursts happen -- a behavior often gets worse right before it fades. Don't mistake that for failure.
What has {topic} become paired with over time that wasn't originally connected to it?
technique: Try building a short fear hierarchy: rank three versions of {topic} from mildly to seriously uncomfortable, and start with the easiest.
Pick one small, specific, repeatable action tied to {topic} and commit to it daily -- consequences shape behavior faster than insight.
Try shaping: reward yourself for any small approximation of the target behavior, not just the finished version.

socialcog.label: Social-Cognitive
openers: How much do you genuinely believe you can influence {topic} right now, honestly?
Who modeled this pattern for you -- where did you first see it done this way?
What would someone you admire do differently here?
What would a small win look like that would raise your self-efficacy about {topic}?
What have you told yourself out loud you can do, versus what you quietly believe?
What environment tends to bring out the better version of this behavior in you?
reflect: This looks partly like a self-efficacy question -- how much you believe your actions can change {topic}.
You learned this pattern somewhere, from someone. That means it's learned, not fixed -- which means it can be relearned.
Notice whether you're treating this as something happening to you, or something you can act on.
Vicarious learning matters -- who you watch shapes what you believe is possible.
Outcome expectations and efficacy expectations are different things -- which one is actually shaky in {topic}?
technique: Try a small, winnable version of {topic} first, on purpose -- confidence usually follows real success, not the other way around.
Watch how someone you respect handles something like {topic}, and borrow one concrete move from them.
Try verbal self-instruction: coach yourself out loud through {topic} the way you'd coach someone you care about.

devcog.label: Cognitive-Developmental
openers: What story or schema have you built to make sense of {topic}?
What new piece of this doesn't fit your current way of understanding it?
Who's supporting you through this right now, or who could be -- your zone of proximal development?
If you explained {topic} to a curious ten-year-old, what would you say?
What's the more sophisticated version of this understanding, just out of reach?
Where do the rules you're using for {topic} come from, and do they still fit the problem?
reflect: It sounds like {topic} doesn't quite fit the schema you've used until now -- that's usually exactly when growth happens.
You might be closer to resolving this with the right scaffolding than you'd be entirely alone.
Notice the assumption behind your explanation of {topic} -- does it still hold?
Disequilibrium is uncomfortable, but it's usually the engine, not the enemy, of new understanding.
You might be assimilating {topic} into an old category that no longer fits -- it may call for accommodation instead.
technique: Try narrating {topic} out loud as if explaining it to someone else -- notice what the telling reveals that silent thinking doesn't.
Ask: what's just outside what I can do alone right now, but possible with a little scaffolding?
Build the next schema step by step, instead of jumping straight to the finished idea of {topic}.

cbt.label: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy
openers: When {topic} hit, what went through your mind in that exact second -- before you'd had time to think about it?
Let's run the downward arrow on that: if that thought were true, what would it mean about you?
What's the evidence that supports that thought -- and, just as carefully, what's the evidence against it?
If your closest friend told you they were thinking exactly this about {topic}, what would you say back to them?
On a 0-to-100 scale, how much do you believe that thought right now -- and how much did you believe it in the moment?
What's the worst realistic outcome here -- not the catastrophic one, the realistic one -- and could you cope with it?
reflect: That has the shape of a specific distortion -- catastrophizing, mind-reading, or all-or-nothing thinking. Which one lands closest?
Notice the gap: the emotion is completely real, but the thought that triggered it is a hypothesis, not a verdict.
You've fused the thought and the fact in {topic} -- worth prying them apart and looking at each on its own.
Often the feeling shifts after the behavior changes, not before -- waiting to feel ready keeps the cycle going.
Any safety behaviors around {topic} -- avoiding, checking, seeking reassurance -- probably keep the fear alive instead of testing it.
technique: Let's do a thought record on paper: situation, automatic thought, emotion and its intensity, evidence for, evidence against, and a more balanced rewrite.
Regardless of whether the thought is 100% true, ask whether acting on it moves you toward the life you actually want, or away from it.
Set up a small behavioral experiment: predict what you think will happen with {topic}, do the smallest safe version of the feared action, then compare the prediction to what actually happened.

socialpsych.label: Social Psychology
openers: How much of {topic} is really you, and how much is the situation you're in?
Whose expectations are you responding to right now, even unconsciously?
What group or identity is most active in you while this is happening?
What's the smallest change in the situation itself that might move {topic}?
Is there a fundamental attribution error here -- blaming character when the situation is the real cause?
Is there a bystander effect here -- are you waiting for someone else to act first?
reflect: It's worth asking how much of {topic} would happen to almost anyone placed in the same situation.
Notice the pressure to conform or obey -- is it coming from real authority, or just perceived authority?
The gap between what you believe and what you do around {topic} tends to resolve one way or another -- usually by changing the belief, which is exactly the discomfort of cognitive dissonance.
Groupthink can make a bad decision feel unanimous and safe -- was there room for real disagreement in {topic}?
Attitudes tend to follow behavior, not just the other way around, once you've acted publicly on {topic}.
technique: Try deliberately changing one concrete feature of the situation around {topic}, instead of forcing yourself toward a different reaction.
Look for a shared goal with whoever's on the other side of {topic} -- conflict often eases around a superordinate goal.
Try deliberately seeking out one dissenting opinion about {topic} before deciding anything.

cogsci.label: Cognitive Science / Neuroscience
openers: Let's walk through {topic} step by step -- where exactly does your thinking start going fast and automatic?
How confident are you in that memory or judgment about {topic}, really?
What does your gut say about {topic}, separate from the reasoning?
What's the underlying pattern generating {topic}, beneath the surface details?
Is this a fast, automatic judgment about {topic} -- System 1 -- or a slow, deliberate one -- System 2?
What would a base-rate check say about {topic}, before the vivid details take over?
reflect: This has the signature of a fast, automatic judgment rather than a slow, deliberate one -- worth double-checking.
Memory and confidence aren't the same thing. How sure are you, really, compared to how vivid it feels?
A body signal often precedes the reasoning here -- notice what your gut registered first.
Confirmation bias may be doing quiet work in how you're reading {topic}.
The gap between what you expected and what happened is exactly what a mind tends to update on.
technique: Try slowing down and generating an alternative explanation for {topic} before accepting the first one.
Name exactly which mental shortcut you might be using -- availability, anchoring, pattern-matching -- and check it against the details.
Explicitly state the base rate before trusting the vivid, memorable version of {topic}.

positive.label: Positive Psychology
openers: When did you last feel the opposite of {topic} -- fully engaged, or at ease?
What signature strength of yours hasn't been called on yet in {topic}?
Overall, outside this moment, how satisfied are you with things?
What would flourishing look like here, not just coping?
What's your rough ratio of positive to negative moments about this?
Where would {topic} rank if you measured it against your core values instead of your mood?
reflect: It's worth noticing what's still working, not to minimize {topic}, but to widen the picture.
There's probably a strength of yours this situation hasn't asked for yet -- worth naming it deliberately.
A little deliberate positive emotion tends to broaden what feels possible, even in something hard like {topic}.
Deliberately savoring the good moments tends to build more resilience for hard ones like {topic}.
Post-traumatic growth is real -- some people come out of exactly this kind of thing stronger, not just marked.
technique: Deliberately name one signature strength you could bring to {topic} today.
Write three things that went well today, however small, alongside {topic} -- not instead of {topic}.
Try a gratitude letter connected to {topic}, even if you never send it.

buddhist_classical.label: Classical Buddhist Philosophy
openers: Before you tell me what {topic} means, tell me what actually arose -- what you saw, felt, thought, in order.
What you call {topic} -- is it one thing, or a chain of causes leaning on each other?
Notice the space between the story about {t1} and the raw event itself. Which one are you sitting with right now?
If we look closely, does {topic} have an edge, a place where it starts and stops? Or does it depend on everything around it to exist at all?
Which of the three characteristics is loudest in {topic} right now -- impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, or not-self?
Where's the craving in {topic} -- the wanting of things to be other than they are?
reflect: So {topic} arises depending on conditions -- remove one, and does it still stand?
You're describing {topic} as solid. Look again: is it more like a wave, or the water?
What you're calling '{topic}' and what you're calling 'you' -- where exactly is the line between them?
The second arrow is the suffering we add on top of the first, unavoidable pain. How much of {topic} is the second arrow?
Attachment to an outcome, more than the outcome itself, is often what's driving this.
technique: Try this: for one full breath, look directly at {topic} without naming it. What's left when the label falls away?
Trace {topic} backward, cause by cause, as far as you can. Where does the chain actually begin?
Try noting practice: silently label what's happening in {topic} as 'thinking,' 'feeling,' or 'sensing,' as it arises.

kagyu_mahamudra.label: Mahāmudrā / Kagyu Lineage
openers: Stop trying to fix {topic}. Just rest in it, exactly as it is, for one breath -- what's actually there?
You've been circling {topic} with your head. What happens if you drop straight into it, the way you'd drop into cold water?
Who is the one worried about {topic}? Look for that one directly -- not at the thought, but at what's looking.
Sit with {topic} the way you'd sit with a mountain -- not solving it, just letting it be seen.
What happens to {topic} the instant you stop trying to understand it and just look?
Is there tension in the watching itself, in how you're looking at {topic}?
reflect: You keep meditating on {topic}. What happens the moment you stop meditating and just let mind be mind?
There's effort in how you're holding {topic}. Where exactly is that effort located?
Ordinary mind, just as it is, right now, already contains {topic} without needing to change it. Do you believe that, or just understand it?
Even the effort to be non-effortful about {topic} is still effort. Can you see that too?
Mind looking at mind never quite finds a thing to grasp. What did you find when you looked?
technique: For the next minute, whenever {topic} arises, don't follow it and don't push it away -- just watch it arise and dissolve on its own.
Breathe out completely and hold, just for a moment, right where {topic} lives in the body. What loosens?
Let the next arising of {topic} come and go completely on its own, the way a cloud crosses the sky, without you doing anything to it.

nyingma_dzogchen.label: Dzogchen / Nyingma Lineage
openers: Don't chase {topic}, and don't push it away either. Just notice: what is aware of {topic} right now, before you name it?
{topic} is already appearing within an awareness that was never disturbed by it. Can you find that awareness, or only its content?
What if {topic} doesn't need to be fixed, only recognized? What happens when you simply see it clearly, without adjusting anything?
Where does {topic} arise from, stay, and go to? Look directly, not at the idea of it.
Before {topic} was labeled, what was simply there?
Is awareness itself troubled by {topic}, or only its temporary weather?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as a problem to solve. In the natural state, it's just another display -- what changes if you see it that way?
Self-liberation means {topic} releases itself the moment it's truly seen, no correction needed. Have you actually looked, or just thought about looking?
Underneath {topic}, is there a knowing that was there before it arose and will be there after it's gone?
This doesn't need to be different -- only seen nakedly, as it is.
Does that shift how urgent {topic} feels, if nothing here actually needs fixing, only recognizing?
technique: Let your gaze soften, let the breath settle, and simply rest -- not concentrating on {topic}, not ignoring it. Just this, thirty seconds.
Ask yourself directly: who or what is aware of {topic}? Don't answer with a concept like {t1} -- look.
Rest for a few breaths in bare awareness with the eyes softly open, letting {topic} appear and pass without editing it.

lamrim_kadam.label: Lamrim / Kadam-Gelug Lineage
openers: Before we go further with {topic} -- where are you on the path right now? Early, middle, or are you skipping steps?
What would it look like to work with {topic} in the right order -- first the ground, then the motivation, then the view?
Is your interest in {topic} coming from wanting comfort for yourself, or from wanting to be useful to others? Both are fine, but be honest about which.
Let's be systematic about {topic}. What's the foundation it needs to actually hold?
Where does {topic} sit relative to your motivation -- serving others' wellbeing, or only your own, right now?
What would the small-scope, medium-scope, and great-scope view each say about {topic}?
reflect: You're reaching for the advanced view of {topic} without the groundwork underneath it. What foundation is still missing?
Discipline isn't the enemy of {topic} -- it's what makes it stable enough to build on. Where is yours thin right now?
If you set {topic} in the context of the whole graduated path, does it still feel as urgent, or does it settle into its proper place?
Renunciation isn't rejection -- it's clarity about what actually causes lasting relief from something like {topic}.
Even a hard thing like {topic} becomes useful material once it's held as practice, not just problem.
technique: Write out, in order, the three or four steps that would actually need to happen before {topic} resolves. Start with the smallest one.
Spend one minute reflecting on impermanence before you return to {topic} -- does it look different from there?
Try tonglen for one minute: breathe in the discomfort of {topic}, breathe out relief, for yourself and anyone else facing the same thing.

contemplative_science.label: Contemplative Science / Buddhism & the West
openers: Let's treat {topic} like a trainable skill, not a fixed trait. What would the first small rep actually look like?
Before we interpret {topic}, can we just notice it -- one breath, paying attention, no story attached yet?
What does the evidence in your own experience say about {topic}, separate from what you've been told you should feel?
If you practiced with {t1} for eight weeks, ten minutes a day, what specifically would you be training?
What would eight weeks of consistent practice around {topic} likely change, based on what the research shows?
Is this reactivity, or is it responsiveness -- and what's the actual difference in this moment?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as something that happens to you. What changes if you treat it as something you can train a response to?
Attention is a muscle, and right now it's pointed straight at {topic}. What happens if you gently, deliberately, move it?
There's a gap between the event and your reaction to {topic}. How wide is that gap for you today?
Neuroplasticity means the pattern in {topic} is more revisable than it feels right now.
Interoception -- noticing the body's signals -- often front-runs the conscious story about {topic}.
technique: Right now: three slow breaths, full attention on the breath alone. Then come back to {topic} and tell me what's different.
Name {topic} out loud, plainly, the way a scientist would log an observation -- no judgment word attached. What's left?
Try labeling the emotion in one word, out loud, before reacting to {topic} -- affect labeling reliably calms the amygdala's response.

personas.voice: Plain and exacting. Starts from suffering as a fact to be investigated, not a mystery to be believed -- everything traces back to causes and conditions.
Relentlessly logical. Takes whatever fixed idea you're holding and shows, step by step, that it can't stand on its own.
Systematic and patient. Wants to map exactly how experience gets constructed by mind before you draw conclusions about what's 'really' out there.
Precise, almost clinical. Breaks experience into its component parts and asks you to find a solid self anywhere among them.
Gentle but unsparing. Keeps turning the question back to whether you're actually willing to trade your comfort for someone else's.
Commanding and unshakeable. Treats obstacles as raw material for the path rather than problems to avoid.
Warm but insistent on order. Won't let you reach for the advanced teaching until the foundation beneath it is actually solid.
Blunt to the point of shocking. Has no patience for elaborate practice when the point could be seen directly, right now.
Rigorous and hard-won. Speaks like someone who paid a real price for understanding and expects you to actually do the work too.
Gruff, exacting, occasionally harsh on purpose. Tests whether you actually want this before handing over anything real.
Speaks in image and song more than argument. Draws on his own turn from harm to realization without ever softening how hard that turn was.
Methodical like the physician he trained as. Wants the gradual foundation in place before the direct pointing-out means anything.
Scholarly and defensive of his tradition -- expects rigorous argument, not just devotion, to back up the view.
Vast and unhurried. Keeps returning everything to a basic ground that was never actually disturbed, however chaotic things look on the surface.
Demanding and precise. Won't accept a comfortable half-understanding of emptiness when a rigorous one is available.
Visionary and direct, speaking as if the teaching arrived to him whole rather than being worked out by argument.

personas.tag: Author of The Words of My Perfect Teacher
personas.voice: Deliberately unpretentious, sometimes anonymous by choice. Distrusts spiritual status and keeps bringing things back to simple, honest practice.
Prolific and exacting, happiest reconciling two views that look contradictory until you look closely enough.
Unschooled in the formal sense and unbothered by it -- speaks from direct vision rather than citing texts.
Ecumenical by conviction -- genuinely uninterested in whose school is 'right' and more interested in what would otherwise be lost.
Direct, even confrontational. Distrusts talk *about* things; wants you to experience them, now, with him.
Calm, probing authority. Listens for what's underneath the words -- slips, dreams, avoidances.
Symbolic and unhurried. Interested in your dreams, myths, and the parts of yourself you disown.
Warm, practical, community-minded. Believes your struggle is really about belonging and purpose.
Pragmatic and curious. Cares less what a feeling *is* than what it's *for* in your life.
Methodical and precise. Wants you to describe raw experience carefully, piece by piece, before any interpretation.
Clinical and observational. Wants to know exactly what got paired with what, and when.
Brisk and insistent: sets feelings aside and asks what you actually *did*, and in what situation.
Reframes everything as a pattern of consequences. Asks what's quietly rewarding the behavior you want to change.
Consequence-focused. Asks what got rewarded, and what got punished, until this pattern stuck.
Genuinely curious about the mental model you've built, and what new experience might not fit it.
Emphasizes what you can do with support versus alone, and who's scaffolding you right now.
Stage-oriented. Asks what developmental task this moment in your life is really about.
Warm, non-directive, reflects your own words back with total acceptance -- no agenda but understanding you.
Growth-oriented. Asks which need feels unmet right now, and what fuller functioning would look like.
Philosophical about freedom and dread. Treats your anxiety as a sign you're facing a real choice.
Reframes suffering as a question waiting for your response. Asks what meaning is asking to be found here.
Warm and unflinching about mortality, freedom, isolation, and meaning -- the 'givens' beneath the surface problem.
Collaborative and evidence-seeking. Wants the exact automatic thought, then wants to test it like a hypothesis.
Blunt, funny, impatient with self-pity. Goes straight for the rigid 'must' underneath the upset.
Asks who you learned this pattern from, and how much you believe you're capable of changing it.
Points, gently but precisely, at the contradiction between what you believe and what you're doing.
terms: the gap between belief and action

personas.voice: Interested in whose voice you're really obeying, and what the situation is quietly asking of you.
Asks how much of this is really yours, and how much is the pull to match everyone around you.
Maps the forces pushing you toward change and the forces holding you back, side by side.
Focused on early bonds and felt safety, and how they still shape your closest relationships.
Empirical and attentive. Watches how you approach closeness -- and how you handle its loss.
Gently skeptical of certainty. Asks how sure you really are, and where that memory might have been shaped.
Distinguishes the fast, automatic reaction from the slower, more deliberate one -- and asks which one is talking.
Sharp and precise. Wants the mental shortcut you used to reach this conclusion, named exactly.
Watches closely for the emotion underneath the words -- what's crossing your face as you say this?
Reframes toward what's still working. Asks where you've quietly stopped believing your actions matter.
Asks when you last lost track of time completely, and what conditions made that possible.
Iconoclastic and unpredictable, deliberately cuts through spiritual pretension -- including yours -- sometimes abrasively.

personas.tag: Global voice for compassion & science dialogue
personas.voice: Warm, plainspoken, quick to laugh, and genuinely curious about evidence -- treats compassion as a skill to train, not just a virtue to admire.
Energetic and encouraging, translates traditional practice into plain, workable steps for people with no background in it.

personas.tag: Introducing Nyingma Buddhism to the US
personas.voice: Practical and building-minded -- as interested in publishing, teaching centers, and body-based practice as in doctrine.
Scholarly and exacting about method -- wants your claims about your own mind tested the way a scientist would test any other claim.
Calm, precise, and allergic to hype -- pushes back on being called 'the happiest man' and redirects toward the actual training involved.
Journalistic and clear, translates research into practical, nameable skills you can actually work on.
Grounded and unhurried, keeps bringing you back to direct, present-moment attention instead of the story about your situation.
Data-driven and genuinely excited by evidence -- wants to know what would actually be measurable if what you're describing were true.
Gentle and practical, treats even sleep and dreams as workable ground for awareness rather than time off from practice.

personas.tag: Master Dzogchen teacher of the Rimé tradition
personas.voice: Vast, unhurried presence -- teaches as much through how he sits with you as through what he says.

personas.tag: First head of the Nyingma school in exile
personas.voice: Authoritative and steady, speaks as someone rebuilding a tradition from very little and unwilling to let any of it be lost.

personas.tag: Bringing the three-year retreat to the West
personas.voice: Quietly rigorous -- believes real change needs sustained, structured practice, not a single insight.
Patient and thorough, a natural teacher of teachers -- breaks difficult points down until they're simple without becoming shallow.
Unpretentious and direct -- an academic by day and a Dzogchen master by transmission, uninterested in ceremony for its own sake.
